questions.prompt: In Doverfield's CRM+ERP integration, what does deciding 'system of record' per data domain actually mean?
options: The ERP owns every field on every shared object, with no exceptions
Salesforce owns every field on every shared object, with no exceptions
Each data domain (e.g., pricing, sales relationship) is assigned exactly one system authorized to originate changes to it, decided field by field where objects are shared
Whichever system saves a record first automatically becomes its system of record
questions.explain: System-of-record decisions are made per data domain, often field by field on a shared object -- not as a blanket rule assigning one system ownership of everything.
questions.distractorExplain: Options A and B describe a blanket, all-or-nothing assignment, which is exactly what Lesson 1 argues against -- Doverfield's Account record has some fields owned by the ERP and others owned by Salesforce, decided individually.

questions.prompt: Why does Doverfield use an event-driven pattern (Platform Events) rather than a synchronous request-reply callout to create a sales order in the ERP when an Opportunity closes?
options: Order creation needs to be reliable but shouldn't block or risk failing the transaction that closed the deal in Salesforce
Event-driven integration is always faster than request-reply in every case
The ERP does not support receiving synchronous callouts under any circumstances
Platform Events are required for every integration regardless of latency needs
questions.explain: The deal-closing transaction shouldn't wait on the ERP's response -- firing an event decouples reliable-but-not-instant order creation from the user's immediate close action.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a Salesforce field marked as an ________ can be used with upsert to reliably insert or update a record using another system's own key, without first querying to determine which case applies.
questions.explain: External ID fields are the mechanism that lets upsert match records reliably across systems using a stable key, rather than a human-readable field like a name.

questions.prompt: Why does an incremental extract filtered only on SystemModstamp fail to capture a deleted record when syncing Salesforce data into Doverfield's warehouse?
options: SystemModstamp only applies to custom objects
A deleted row no longer exists to be returned by any query filtering for recently-changed rows, since it's gone rather than merely changed
Deleted records are automatically restored after a short delay
SystemModstamp cannot be used in Bulk API queries
questions.explain: A query can only return rows that still exist -- a deleted record is absent from the result set entirely, which is exactly the gap Change Data Capture's delete events are built to close.

questions.prompt: In Doverfield's employee SSO design, what role does Salesforce play relative to the corporate Identity Provider, and what field does the SAML configuration use to map identity?
options: Salesforce is the Identity Provider; it maps identity using the Salesforce password
Salesforce is the Service Provider, trusting the IdP's signed SAML assertion; it maps identity using the Federation ID field rather than username
Salesforce and the IdP both independently validate the user's password with no trust relationship
Salesforce is the Service Provider, but identity mapping always uses the Salesforce username
questions.explain: Salesforce acts as the Service Provider trusting the IdP's assertion, and Doverfield deliberately maps identity via Federation ID -- a stable, dedicated key -- rather than username, which can change.

questions.prompt: Why can't Just-in-Time (JIT) provisioning be used to deactivate a Salesforce user who has left the company?
options: JIT has a dedicated deactivation setting Doverfield simply hasn't enabled
A disabled or deactivated Salesforce user will not complete SAML authentication at all, so JIT has no login event to act on -- deactivation requires a separate offboarding step
SAML assertions cannot carry any information about terminated employees
JIT provisioning only works for creating accounts, never for any kind of account update
questions.explain: JIT's mechanism is tied to a successful login event -- a deactivated user can't log in at all, so there's no event for JIT to act on, which is why deactivation needs its own separate process.

questions.prompt: Match each Doverfield customer-portal sharing concept to what it actually does.
right: The platform used to build the external-facing portal itself
The baseline record-level access before any sharing mechanism adds to it; must be Private for this pattern to work safely
The record that associates an external user with their Account
An account-based access mapping that automatically shares matching records with external users, configured once
questions.explain: OWD sets the private baseline. A sharing set then grants account-matched access automatically. The Contact record is what ties an external user to their Account. Experience Cloud is the platform hosting the whole portal.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a single Apex transaction can make up to ________ callouts in total, and all callouts in that transaction share a combined cumulative timeout of 120 seconds.
questions.explain: Salesforce's Execution Governors and Limits reference sets the total callout count per transaction at 100, with a shared 120-second cumulative timeout across all of them.

questions.prompt: Why is a field-level ownership matrix necessary even after a domain-level system-of-record split (like 'the ERP owns pricing') is already in place?
options: Domain-level ownership doesn't specify who owns each individual shared field on a shared object like Account, leaving that as an implicit, unreviewed assumption
Field-level matrices are a Salesforce licensing requirement
Domain-level ownership only applies to custom objects, never standard objects
Field-level ownership replaces the need for External IDs entirely
questions.explain: A shared object can have many fields with different natural owners -- the domain-level split doesn't resolve ownership field by field, which is exactly the gap an explicit field-level matrix closes.

questions.prompt: What is 'silent last-write-wins,' and why does this course treat it as a failure mode rather than a legitimate conflict-resolution strategy?
options: It's an outcome where nobody explicitly chose a conflict rule, and the sync job's accidental execution order ends up deciding the result -- an unreviewed side effect, not a deliberate policy
It's a documented Salesforce feature recommended for all shared fields
It's a setting that disables error notifications for failed sync jobs
It only happens when an object has no External ID field defined at all
questions.explain: The distinction is intent: a deliberately chosen last-write-wins rule with trustworthy timestamps is a real policy, while silent last-write-wins is an unreviewed accident that happens to look fine until two near-simultaneous updates expose it.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Doverfield's retry-and-recovery design for its ERP sync.
options: Retry with exponential backoff waits progressively longer between attempts, up to a capped maximum, rather than retrying immediately and indefinitely
A dead-letter queue gives a failed message, once retries are exhausted, a visible, recoverable home instead of disappearing or retrying forever
Idempotency (via upsert on a stable External ID) is what makes retrying a call safe, since a retry of an already-successful call lands on the same record instead of creating a duplicate
Immediate, unlimited retries are the recommended approach because they resolve outages the fastest
A scheduled reconciliation job is unnecessary once retry and dead-letter handling are in place
questions.explain: Backoff avoids overloading an already-struggling system, dead-letter queues give failures a recoverable home, and idempotency makes retries safe. Immediate unlimited retries make outages worse, and reconciliation remains necessary as a separate safety net for drift retries and dead-letter handling don't catch.

questions.prompt: What problem does PK Chunking solve for Doverfield's Bulk API extraction of a very large object like Opportunity History?
options: It automatically splits a large query into smaller batches scoped to ranges of the object's record IDs, so the extraction processes the object in manageable pieces rather than as one enormous query
It encrypts extracted data at rest automatically
It eliminates the need for query selectivity entirely
It converts an asynchronous Bulk API job into a synchronous REST call
questions.explain: PK Chunking breaks a very large extraction into smaller ID-range-scoped batches, which becomes relevant once an object's volume is large enough that a single unchunked query risks becoming the job's own bottleneck.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Change Data Capture does not retain its event stream forever -- events are only available for a subscriber to replay within a bounded ________, after which an unconsumed event is gone for good.
questions.explain: If a subscriber falls behind or goes down for longer than the CDC retention window, the changes that occurred during that gap become permanently unrecoverable through CDC alone, which is why Doverfield relies on scheduled reconciliation as a backstop.

questions.prompt: Match each async Apex pattern to the situation this course says it fits best.
right: Processing a large number of records through a callout-driven process in controlled-size chunks
A simple, independent callout with no need to chain into further async work
Failing fast against a persistently failing external dependency instead of waiting out full timeouts
A callout result that needs to trigger a second, dependent async step, with more complex input than primitives
questions.explain: Future methods fit simple independent callouts. Queueable supports chaining and richer input. Batch Apex fits large-volume chunked processing. A circuit breaker is a resilience pattern that fails fast once failures cross a threshold, regardless of which async mechanism is underneath it.

questions.prompt: In this course's comparison matrix across Doverfield's five case studies, what actually tracks the pattern choice (synchronous vs. event-driven vs. batch) more tightly than raw data volume?
options: The primary risk if that specific integration fails -- low-volume cases with severe failure modes (like identity/login lockout) get real-time handling, while high-volume cases with mild failure modes (like a stale dashboard) can tolerate delay
The number of Apex classes written for each integration
Which case study was built first chronologically
The number of fields shared between the two systems involved
questions.explain: Failure-risk severity, not data volume, explains why the lowest-volume case (identity) needed synchronous handling while the highest-volume case (the warehouse) could tolerate hours of staleness.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about this course's security-and-governance review lens, as distinct from the design-comparison lens.
options: Keeping secrets out of Apex code via Named Credentials is necessary but not sufficient -- who can view or edit the Named Credential setup records themselves is a separate governance question
Shield Platform Encryption and field-level security answer the same question and are redundant with each other
Event Monitoring helps answer 'if this happens, do we know about it,' which access controls like sharing sets don't address on their own
The security/governance review and the design-comparison review are redundant passes that should be combined into one
A compromised or misconfigured integration user quietly over-exporting data is the kind of incident Event Monitoring is specifically meant to help catch
questions.explain: Named Credential access governance, Event Monitoring's after-the-fact visibility, and catching integration-user abuse are all real, distinct governance concerns. Shield encryption and field-level security are complementary, not redundant, and the two review lenses (design-comparison vs. security/governance) are explicitly described as orthogonal, not redundant.

questions.prompt: What is 'requirements traceability' when presenting an integration design to a review board?
options: Listing every field mapping used in the integration for completeness
Being able to trace every significant design decision back to a specific, previously-stated requirement or constraint, rather than leaving the connection implicit
Tracking how long each Apex class takes to execute in production
Writing every requirement in formal UML notation before presenting
Only including requirements that were met without any tradeoffs
Ensuring the diagram contains no more than five boxes
questions.explain: Traceability means the reviewer doesn't have to guess why a decision was made -- each decision explicitly connects back to a stated need, such as Doverfield's event-driven ERP sync tracing back to its delay-tolerance requirement.
questions.distractorExplain: Option A describes documentation completeness, not traceability -- a field-mapping list doesn't by itself show why any decision was made. Traceability is specifically about connecting a decision to the requirement that justified it, not about exhaustively cataloguing implementation detail.

questions.prompt: Per this course's objection-handling lesson, what is the strongest way to respond when a design genuinely has no good answer to a scaling objection like '10x data volume'?
options: Say so plainly, and name the specific change needed to close the gap, such as moving an object from scheduled incremental extract to CDC
Pretend the design already handles it without naming any specific change
Avoid answering the question entirely
Claim data volume never actually grows in real Salesforce orgs
questions.explain: An honest gap admission paired with a concrete fix is explicitly called out as a stronger answer than pretending a design handles something it doesn't -- this is the same honest-gap-admission pattern the course reuses at the portfolio level.

questions.prompt: Per this course's mock review board lesson, what does a review panel score beyond whether the candidate's final technical answer was correct?
options: Only the visual quality of the presentation slides
How the candidate reasoned and defended each answer -- conceding valid points, connecting answers back to established criteria, and having actual evidence rather than just confidence
The total number of objections the candidate can correctly predict in advance
Whether the candidate used the exact same wording as the course material
questions.explain: A candidate who answers correctly but argues defensively or invents justifications on the spot scores worse than one who reasons visibly and honestly, even if their final answers require more humility.

questions.prompt: Per this course's final lesson, what is the difference between a 'credibility gap' and an acceptable 'future-work gap' in an architecture portfolio?
options: A credibility gap is a gap in an area the portfolio's own narrative claims to have already covered (undermining trust); a future-work gap is honestly named with a stated plan, which can actually strengthen the portfolio
There is no real difference -- both types of gap are equally damaging to a portfolio
A credibility gap only occurs in Chapter 1, while a future-work gap only occurs in Chapter 3
A future-work gap must always be closed before presenting, while a credibility gap can be left open indefinitely
questions.explain: The key distinction is whether the gap contradicts a claim the portfolio makes. Claiming a design is 'fully resilient' while never describing its resilience mechanism is a credibility gap; honestly naming an untested area with a plan to close it is an acceptable, even strengthening, future-work gap.
